issues.legal_issue: Testimony from a witness related to the victim is not inherently unreliable or liable to be rejected solely because of that relationship.
material_facts: The two eyewitnesses whose testimony the court accepted were the victim’s son and wife, and their presence at the scene was natural because the incident occurred outside their home in the morning.
Their accounts were consistent, cogent, and reliable, and the defence did not establish a motive to falsely implicate the accused.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitnesses’ testimony could not be disbelieved merely because they were close relatives of the victim.
issues.legal_principle: A related witness is not necessarily an interested witness. A witness is interested when the witness has a benefit or direct or indirect interest in the outcome, such as a motive arising from enmity to secure punishment by false implication. The court should cautiously assess a related witness’s testimony for reliability, probability, cogency, and consistency, but should not treat it as inherently tainted. The court relied on State of Rajasthan v. Kalki, (1981) 2 SCC 752; Amit v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2012) 4 SCC 107; Gangabhavani v. Rayapati Venkat Reddy, (2013) 15 SCC 298; Ganapathi v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2018) 5 SCC 549; Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, 1954 SCR 145; and Jayabalan v. Union Territory of Pondicherry, (2010) 1 SCC 199.

rule.if: criminal_case and witness_is_related and witness_presence_is_natural and testimony_is_reliable and not evidence_of_motive_to_falsely_implicate

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the determination of criminal liability.
predicates.witness_is_related: The witness is related to the victim.
predicates.witness_presence_is_natural: The circumstances explain why the witness was naturally present at the scene.
predicates.testimony_is_reliable: The witness’s testimony is consistent, cogent, and reliable on the material events.
predicates.evidence_of_motive_to_falsely_implicate: Evidence shows that the witness had a motive to falsely implicate the accused.

issues.definition: When a related witness was naturally present, gives reliable testimony, and no motive to falsely implicate is shown, the testimony is not rejected solely because of the relationship.

issues.legal_issue: Minor variations or discrepancies that do not affect the core of the prosecution case do not by themselves make otherwise reliable eyewitness testimony unacceptable.
material_facts: The son’s and wife’s accounts of the assault were consistent on the material events.
The court found no major contradiction, and the defence did not elicit a material contradiction in cross-examination.
Any variations were minor and concerned trivial matters.
issues.conclusion: The minor variations did not justify rejecting the eyewitness testimony.
issues.legal_principle: Minor discrepancies on trivial matters do not in and of themselves affect the core of the prosecution case, and evidence should not be rejected solely because of such variations.

rule.if: criminal_case and eyewitness_testimony_is_reliable and discrepancies_are_minor and discrepancies_do_not_affect_core_case

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the determination of criminal liability.
predicates.eyewitness_testimony_is_reliable: The eyewitness accounts are otherwise consistent and reliable on the material events.
predicates.discrepancies_are_minor: The differences in the accounts concern minor or trivial matters rather than material events.
predicates.discrepancies_do_not_affect_core_case: The differences do not undermine the central account of the prosecution case.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, minor differences in otherwise reliable eyewitness accounts do not invalidate the testimony when those differences leave the core case unaffected.

issues.legal_issue: A reliable dying declaration may support a conviction without corroboration, and corroboration by reliable evidence further supports reliance on it.
material_facts: The victim gave a statement to the doctor who first treated him, and the doctor testified that the victim was in a fit state of mind when making it.
The doctor supported the recording of the statement, and the court found no material showing that the victim was tutored or prompted or that the statement was fabricated.
The reliable eyewitness testimony corroborated the declaration in all material particulars.
issues.conclusion: The dying declaration was reliable and could be relied on as evidence supporting the conviction.
issues.legal_principle: There is no absolute rule that a dying declaration cannot be the sole basis of conviction unless corroborated. A declaration may be relied on if it is reliable and is not an attempt to conceal the truth or falsely implicate the accused; corroboration by other prosecution evidence provides further support.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the determination of criminal liability.
predicates.dying_declaration_is_reliable: The declaration was made by a person in a fit state of mind and is otherwise found reliable.
predicates.declaration_is_attempt_to_conceal_truth_: The declaration is an attempt to conceal the truth or falsely implicate the accused.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, a reliable dying declaration that is not an attempt to conceal the truth or falsely implicate the accused may support a conviction even without corroboration.

issues.legal_issue: A reversal of an acquittal is justified when the appellate court independently reassesses the evidence, gives reasons, and finds the acquittal based on an implausible view of the case.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused, and the State appealed.
The High Court independently evaluated the evidence, found the trial court’s view implausible in light of the evidence, and gave reasons for reversing the acquittal.
The Supreme Court agreed that there were substantial and compelling reasons to differ from the trial court’s findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal, and there was no valid ground to interfere with its conviction.
issues.legal_principle: On an appeal from an acquittal, the appellate court may reverse the acquittal where, after independent evaluation and by assigning reasons, it finds the acquittal view implausible and substantial and compelling reasons to differ from the trial court. The judgment states this principle without citing a specific earlier case or statutory provision for it.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquittal and appellate_court_independently_reassesses_evidence and acquittal_view_is_implausible and appellate_court_gives_reasons

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.appellate_court_independently_reassesses: The appellate court independently evaluates the evidence and material on record.
predicates.acquittal_view_is_implausible: The appellate court finds that the trial court’s view is not plausible in light of the evidence and circumstances.
predicates.appellate_court_gives_reasons: The appellate court explains its basis for differing from the acquittal.

issues.definition: An appellate court may justifiably reverse an acquittal when it independently reassesses the evidence, finds the acquittal view implausible, and gives reasons for its decision.
